content: The following are professional summaries of the studies and guidelines referenced: 1. Masanja et al. conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Tanzania (NeoVita) to evaluate the impact of neonatal vitamin A supplementation on infant mortality. The findings were published in The Lancet in 2015. 2. Mazumder et al. performed a similar randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Haryana, India, to assess the efficacy of early neonatal vitamin A supplementation in reducing infant mortality. This study was also published in The Lancet in 2015. 3. Ahmad et al. investigated the effects of high-dose neonatal vitamin A supplementation on thymic function during early infancy. Their findings, which indicated a transient decrease in thymic function, were published in The Journal of Nutrition in 2020. 4. Klemm et al. explored the feasibility of delivering vitamin A to newborns in Nepal and Bangladesh. Their findings were published in Sight and Life in 2011. 5. The Codex Alimentarius Commission established a global standard for infant formula and formulas for special medical purposes intended for infants. This standard, originally adopted in 1981, was updated by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2007. 6. Tan et al. reviewed the role of vitamin D supplementation in term breastfed infants to prevent vitamin D deficiency and improve bone health. This systematic review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2020. 7. Chandy et al. conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation, either directly or via breast milk, on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels, related biochemistry, and infection susceptibility in term infants. The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition in 2016. 8. Floreskul et al. modeled the cost-effectiveness of vitamin D supplementation in pregnant women and young children to prevent rickets. Their study was published in Frontiers in Public Health in 2020. 9. Roth et al. provided a comprehensive analysis of the global prevalence and disease burden of vitamin D deficiency, with a focus on lowand middle-income countries. Their roadmap for action was published in Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences in 2018. 10. Wagner and Greer discussed strategies for preventing rickets and vitamin D deficiency in infants, children, and adolescents. Their recommendations were published in Pediatrics in 2008. 11. Simon and Ahrens examined adherence to vitamin D intake guidelines in the United States, with their findings published in Pediatrics in 2020. 12. Umaretiya et al. explored maternal preferences for vitamin D supplementation in breastfed infants. Their study was published in Annals of Family Medicine in 2017. 13. Taylor et al. investigated the use of supplemental vitamin D among infants who were breastfed for prolonged periods. Their findings were published in Pediatrics in 2010. 14. Heinig reviewed controversies and concerns surrounding vitamin D supplementation in breastfed infants. This review was published in Journal of Human Lactation in 2003. 15. The WHO convened a Vitamin D Expert Panel Meeting, which resulted in a final report accessible as of January 2022. 16. Crocker et al. reported high rates of vitamin D supplementation among infants aged two months in Vancouver and Richmond, British Columbia, Canada. Their findings were published in BMC Public Health in 2011. 17. Gallo et al. examined vitamin D supplementation practices among Canadian infants, focusing on Montreal mothers. Their study was published in Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism in 2010. 18. Hemingway et al. assessed adherence to infant vitamin D supplementation policies in Ireland. Their findings were published in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2020. 19. Field reviewed research on pediatric massage therapy, highlighting its benefits for infants. This narrative review was published in Children (Basel) in 2019. 20. Kulkarni et al. summarized evidence on massage and touch therapy in neonates, with their findings published in Indian Pediatrics in 2010. 21. Their study was published in the International Journal of Neuroscience in 2009. 22. Schanberg et al. found that massage with oil has more positive effects on normal infants compared to massage without oil. This study was published in Journal of Prenatal and Perinatal Psychology and Health in 1996. 23. Field provided a comprehensive review of massage therapy research, published in Complementary Therapies in Clinical Practice in 2016. 24. Priyadarshi et al. conducted a systematic review on the effects of whole-body massage on growth and neurodevelopment in term healthy newborns. This review is currently under submission. 25. Bennett et al. reviewed the impact of massage on promoting mental and physical health in typically developing infants under six months of age. Their findings were published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2013. 26. Zhang et al. performed a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to evaluate the influence of massage on neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. Their findings were published in the Journal of Maternal-Fetal & Neonatal Medicine in 2019. 27. Gürol and Polat studied the effects of baby massage on attachment between mothers and their infants. Their findings were published in Asian Nursing Research in 2012. 28. Keller and Rehm conducted a qualitative case study on fathers' experiences with infant massage. Their findings were published in the Journal of Behavioral and Social Sciences in 2015. 29. The WHO published guidelines in 2020 aimed at improving early childhood development. 30. The WHO and UNICEF outlined acceptable medical reasons for the use of breast-milk substitutes in a 2009 publication. 31. The WHO and UNICEF released updated guidelines in 2018 for implementing the revised Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative to support breastfeeding in maternity and newborn care facilities. 32. The WHO established the International Code of Marketing of Breast-Milk Substitutes in 1981 to protect breastfeeding practices globally. 33. Jones et al. conducted a meta-analysis on early postnatal discharge for healthy mothers and term infants, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2021. 34. Yonemoto et al. reviewed schedules for home visits during the early postpartum period, with their findings published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2021. 35. Tiruneh et al. evaluated the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of home-based postpartum care on neonatal mortality and exclusive breastfeeding practices in lowand middle-income countries. Their systematic review and meta-analysis were published in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth in 2019. 36. Bernstein et al. examined the impact of varying perceptions of readiness for postpartum discharge on health outcomes. Their findings were published in Ambulatory Pediatrics in 2002. 37. Dol et al. explored maternal postnatal newborn care education in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, identifying barriers, facilitators, and opportunities. Their study was published in Midwifery in 2019. 38. Malagon-Maldonado et al. identified predictors of readiness for hospital discharge after birth, with their findings published in Worldviews on Evidence-Based Nursing in 2017. 39. Tokhi et al. systematically reviewed the effectiveness of involving men in improving maternal and newborn health. Their findings were published in PLOS One in 2018. 40. José Santos highlighted the MenCare initiative in Latin America, which challenges harmful masculine norms and promotes positive caregiving changes. This case study was published by the Institute of Development Studies in 2015. 41. The WHO released recommendations in 2015 on health promotion interventions for maternal and newborn health. 42. The International Initiative for Impact Evaluation (3ie) published an evidence map in 2017 on social, behavioral, and community engagement interventions for reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health. 43. Ruane-McAteer et al. reviewed interventions addressing men, masculinities, and gender equality in sexual and reproductive health. Their findings were published in BMJ Global Health in 2019. 44. Gunn et al. conducted a randomized trial in Australian general practice to evaluate the impact of early postnatal check-ups on maternal health. Their findings were published in the British Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology in 1998. 45. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) provided guidelines in 2021 on the timing of the first postnatal contact by midwives. 46. Dol et al. reviewed the timing of maternal and neonatal mortality and morbidity during the postnatal period. Their systematic review protocol was published in JBI Evidence Synthesis in 2021. 47. Oza et al. estimated the daily risk of neonatal death, including the day of birth, across 186 countries in 2013. Their study was published in The Lancet Global Health in 2014. 48. Oza et al. provided neonatal cause-of-death estimates for the early and late neonatal periods across 194 countries from 2000 to 2013. Their findings were published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2015. 49. Jones et al. conducted a meta-analysis on early postnatal discharge for infants, with their findings published in Pediatrics in 2020. 50. Sainz Bueno et al. evaluated early discharge from obstetrics-pediatrics with domiciliary follow-up at the Hospital de Valme. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2005. 51. Petrou et al. conducted an economic evaluation comparing home-based care after a shortened hospital stay versus hospital-based postpartum care. Their findings were published in BJOG in 2004. 52. Bowers and Cheyne analyzed the implications of reducing postnatal hospital stay length on cost and quality of care. Their findings were published in BMC Health Services Research in 2016. 53. Benova et al. examined postpartum care provision for women giving birth in health facilities across sub-Saharan Africa. Their cross-sectional study was published in PLOS Medicine in 2019. 54. Doctor et al. analyzed time trends in facility-based and private-sector childbirth care across 25 sub-Saharan African countries from 2000 to 2016. Their findings were published in Journal of Global Health in 2019. 55. Montagu et al. explored the changing landscape of childbirth in Africa and Asia, with their findings published in Health Policy and Planning in 2017. 56. Brooten et al. conducted a randomized trial on early hospital discharge and home follow-up for women undergoing cesarean births. Their findings were published in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 1994. 57. Altuntuğ and Ege evaluated the effects of health education on mothers' readiness for postpartum discharge, postpartum complaints, and quality of life. Their findings were published in the Turkish Journal of Research and Development in Nursing in 2013. 58. Bryanton et al. reviewed postnatal parental education for optimizing infant health and parent-infant relationships. Their findings were published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2013. 59. Rasaily et al. evaluated the effect of home-based newborn care on neonatal and infant mortality in India. Their cluster randomized trial was published in BMJ Global Health in 2020. 60. LeFevre et al. conducted an economic evaluation of neonatal care packages in a cluster-randomized controlled trial in Sylhet, Bangladesh. Their findings were published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2013. 61. Pitt et al. analyzed the cost and cost-effectiveness of newborn home visits in rural Ghana. Their findings were published in The Lancet Global Health in 2016. 62. Daviaud et al. provided an overview of multi-country community-based maternal and newborn care economic analyses. Their findings were published in Health Policy and Planning in 2017. 63. Barger et al. conducted a multi-country analysis of the cost of community health worker kits and commodities for maternal and newborn care. Their findings were published in Health Policy and Planning in 2017. 64. UNICEF, WHO, and the World Bank Group published a report in 2019 on levels and trends in child mortality. 65. Chao et al. systematically assessed national and regional under-5 mortality rates by economic status in lowand middle-income countries. Their findings were published in The Lancet Global Health in 2018. 66. McPherson and Hodgins reviewed lessons from country programs operating at scale for postnatal home visitation. Their findings were published in Journal of Global Health in 2018. 67. Escobar et al. compared home visits and hospital-based group follow-up visits after early postpartum discharge. Their findings were published in Pediatrics in 2001. 68. Lieu et al. conducted a randomized comparison of home and clinic follow-up visits after early postpartum hospital discharge. Their findings were published in Pediatrics in 2000. 69. The WHO released recommendations in 2012 on optimizing health worker roles to improve access to maternal and newborn health interventions through task shifting. 70. The WHO published guidelines in 2019 for malaria vector control. 71. The WHO released a guideline in 2021 on health workforce development, attraction, recruitment, and retention in rural and remote areas. 72. Baguiya et al. are preparing a study on the effectiveness of male involvement interventions on maternal and newborn health outcomes. 73. Kunene et al. explored male involvement in maternity care in South Africa, with their findings published by the Population Council in 2004. 74. The WHO released recommendations in 2018 on home-based records for maternal, newborn, and child health. 75. The WHO published a guideline in 2019 on digital interventions for health system strengthening.
